title: Calculating the ROI of UX
intro: Stakeholders see UX as a 'nice-to-have' until you put a number on it. This 5-step framework turns usability improvements into dollars saved or earned.

learn.title: The 5-step ROI framework
learn.text:
Step 1: **Identify the problem and benchmark it.** Measure the current state — support calls, error rates, time-on-task, conversion.

Step 2: **Define goals and expected outcomes.** Set measurable targets tied to both UX and business results.

Step 3: **Gather data to estimate ROI.** Quantify the Return (time saved, errors reduced, revenue gained) and the Investment (recruitment, team hours, dev cost).

Step 4: **Calculate ROI.** Benefits minus cost, divided by cost. Convert to a dollar figure.

Step 5: **Communicate results.** Lead with the problem, highlight key metrics, be transparent about assumptions.

try.explain: ROI = (Benefit − Cost) ÷ Cost. Then multiply by 100 for a percentage.

learn.title: A real example: support cost reduction
learn.text:
A university redesigned their registration form.

**Before:** 940 support hours per semester on registration issues.
**After:** 280 hours — a drop of 660 hours.

At $26.44/hour, that's **~$17,450 saved per semester.**
Project cost: ~$10,000.

ROI = ($17,450 − $10,000) ÷ $10,000 = **74.5%**
Or: **$1.75 returned per dollar spent.**

This is a conservative, single-metric calculation. The real impact (fewer frustrated students, faster throughput) is even bigger.

try.q: Why is this called a 'conservative' calculation?
options: It only counts one benefit (support hours) and ignores indirect gains
It uses the most expensive hourly rate in the company for every calculation
try.explain: Conservative means you count only the most measurable, direct benefit. The real impact on retention, satisfaction, and throughput is bigger.

learn.title: Communicating ROI to stakeholders
learn.text:
The calculation is useless if nobody acts on it.

**Lead with the number.** "This redesign returns $1.75 for every $1 spent."

**Then tell the story.** Problem → what you did → what changed → what it's worth.

**Be honest about assumptions.** Round down projections, use ranges, base estimates on historical data or benchmarks.

**Triangulate.** Pair the ROI number with qualitative evidence — user quotes, task completion improvements, NPS shifts.

Don't bury the number in a 40-slide deck. Put it on slide 2.

right.label: Don't
items: Bury numbers in a long deck

try.q: You calculated a 200% ROI on a checkout redesign. What goes on slide 2?
options: The ROI number with a one-line problem statement
try.explain: Lead with the number. Stakeholders need the bottom line first, then the story behind it.

test.q: What is the first step in the ROI framework?
options: Identify the problem and establish benchmarks
Present early findings to stakeholders for approval
test.explain: You can't measure improvement without knowing where you started. Benchmark first.

test.q: A redesign saves 500 support hours/year at $30/hour. The project cost $8,000. What's the ROI?
Why should you use conservative estimates when calculating UX ROI?
options: Conservative numbers are easier to calculate
test.explain: If your projections are too optimistic and reality falls short, future UX budget requests suffer. Underpromise, overdeliver. (If you promise 10x and deliver 3x, stakeholders lose trust.)

test.q: What should you pair with ROI numbers when presenting to stakeholders?
options: More ROI numbers from other projects
test.explain: Numbers tell the business story. Qualitative evidence makes it human and credible. Triangulate. (User quotes, task completion data, observed pain points.)

test.q: Which of these counts as 'Investment' in the ROI formula?
options: Team hours, recruitment, development, maintenance, and training costs
The revenue the company lost during the project, plus the forecast for next year
test.explain: Investment includes everything: team time, research recruitment, dev work, maintenance, training, subscriptions. Leave nothing out.
